# Security Considerations for Tool-Calling AI Agents

Building an agent that can invoke external tools introduces a fundamentally different security model than traditional software: the LLM mixes trusted instructions and untrusted data in the same natural-language channel, so classic sanitization boundaries don't hold by default. Considerations break down into five areas.

## 1. Prompt Injection and Trust Boundary Failures

The central risk is that an LLM cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data [sysdig.com](https://www.sysdig.com/learn-cloud-native/prompt-injection). When a tool call returns content from the web, email, tickets, code repos, or databases, hostile instructions embedded in that content can hijack the agent's behavior — causing it to exfiltrate data, take unauthorized actions, or misuse its connected tools [gend.co](https://www.gend.co/en-ca/blog/chatgpt-prompt-injection-defence) [mend.io](https://www.mend.io/blog/2025-owasp-top-10-for-llm-applications-a-quick-guide) [mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/17/1/54). A real-world instance: a prompt injection flaw in GitHub's official MCP server let AI coding assistants read/write repositories without authorization because the agent held broad permissions while processing untrusted content [mend.io](https://www.mend.io/blog/owasp-top-10-for-llm-applications-a-quick-guide). Consequences extend to log/audit corruption (an attacker silently rewriting the agent's task mid-run undermines later reconstruction of intent) and broader compliance/reputational exposure [mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/17/1/54). Industry frameworks now formalize this: OWASP ranks prompt injection as the #1 LLM risk, MITRE ATLAS assigns it technique ID AML.T0051, and a dedicated **OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)** frames instruction abuse, tool misuse, and trust-boundary failures as core application risks — covering hijacked planning leading to privileged tool calls, persistent malicious instructions in memory, and attack propagation across connected systems [nhimg.org](https://nhimg.org/articles/llm-security-risks-in-2026-prompt-injection-mcp-and-agent-abuse) [christian-schneider.net](https://christian-schneider.net/blog/prompt-injection-agentic-amplification). NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act are also cited as governance-level references for mapping these risks [nhimg.org](https://nhimg.org/faq/how-should-security-teams-review-llm-and-agent-code-for-prompt-injection-risks-i).

## 2. Authentication, Authorization, and Permission Scoping

- **Identity**: Use enterprise-standard mechanisms — OAuth 2.0 delegated flows (e.g., Entra On-Behalf-Of) for user-initiated actions, managed identities/service principals for autonomous background agents — rather than privileged, static agent credentials [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/6018383/what-are-the-best-practices-for-securing-ai-agents). Give each agent its own distinct credentials rather than a shared org token, so access can be scoped and revoked independently [scopegate.dev](https://scopegate.dev/blog/ai-agent-least-privilege).
- **Credential handling**: Issue ephemeral, short-lived, tool-scoped tokens rather than long-lived keys. Isolate credentials in a server-side connections/credential-management layer that handles storage, refresh, rotation, and revocation — the agent itself should never touch raw downstream credentials [descope.com](https://www.descope.com/blog/post/ai-agent-credential-management) [nango.dev](https://nango.dev/blog/guide-to-secure-ai-agent-api-authentication).
- **Authorization**: The backend/API, not the agent, must be the final authority — never trust the agent's self-reported permissions. Validate tool calls against defined schemas and business rules at a gateway layer [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/6018383/what-are-the-best-practices-for-securing-ai-agents). Use OAuth scopes plus fine-grained claims, restrict tokens by audience, and use token exchange/transaction tokens so one agent can't pass excessive privilege to another in agent-to-agent scenarios [curity.io](https://curity.io/resources/learn/api-security-best-practice-for-ai-agents).
- **Least privilege**: Scope permissions to the specific operation, resource, identity, and environment (read ≠ write ≠ delete); expose only a limited, explicitly-schema'd set of tools [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/6018383/what-are-the-best-practices-for-securing-ai-agents). Use narrow OAuth scopes (e.g., `gmail.readonly` vs. `mail.google.com`), and add a tool-level permission layer above OAuth since native scopes are often too coarse — this should be a hard, service-enforced boundary, not just a soft limit inside the agent framework, since MCP servers/agent frameworks otherwise expose all tools to every connected agent [scopegate.dev](https://scopegate.dev/blog/ai-agent-least-privilege).
- Require explicit human approval before high-risk/high-privilege actions execute [curity.io](https://curity.io/resources/learn/api-security-best-practice-for-ai-agents).

## 3. Input Validation, Output Sanitization, and Sandboxing

- **Input validation**: Treat all tool parameters as untrusted — validate types/formats, enforce range and size limits (e.g., pagination caps), and screen early in the pipeline for injection attempts, PII, and toxicity before reaching tool-access control [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl) [akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail). Pin versions and verify signatures for plugin/protocol systems like MCP [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl).
- **Output sanitization**: Enforce schema compliance on tool outputs and filter harmful/policy-violating content as a second line of defense before results reach the user or re-enter the agent's context [akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail). Treat agent-generated code/shell commands as untrusted until proven otherwise, routing them through controlled execution [youtube.com](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WruAgVKW0tU).
- **Sandboxing**: Standard containers share a host kernel and are insufficient for executing AI-generated code; stronger isolation (gVisor for syscall interception, or microVMs like Firecracker/Kata Containers for a dedicated kernel per workload) is needed [northflank.com](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents). Effective sandboxing must jointly address code execution exploits, filesystem access, network egress, resource consumption, and privilege escalation via compute limits, filesystem rules, network controls, and scoped short-lived credentials [youtube.com](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WruAgVKW0tU) [northflank.com](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents). Note that sandboxes themselves are increasingly targeted (hypervisor/host OS exploits), so they should not be relied on as a sole control [menlosecurity.com](https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/what-cisos-need-to-know-about-modern-sandboxing-limitations).
- Layer defenses — read-only tools where possible → input validation → egress constraints → caching → circuit breakers → per-request auth → logging — so a single failure doesn't cascade [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl).

## 4. Logging, Monitoring, and Auditing

- Maintain **immutable logs** of every tool invocation, parameter, and approval decision, preserving the full delegation chain (agent identity, authorizing human/policy, reasoning steps) for each action [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl) [kovrr.com](https://www.kovrr.com/blog-post/monitoring-ai-agent-behavior-in-production).
- Continuously monitor for anomalous execution rates, unusual tool-chaining (e.g., a DB read followed by an external transfer), cost/latency outliers, and deviations from behavioral baselines for tool-use patterns — these can signal goal hijacking or abuse [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-agent-goal-hijack-in-ai-agents-4eia) [kovrr.com](https://www.kovrr.com/blog-post/monitoring-ai-agent-behavior-in-production).
- Retain logs per applicable regulatory retention requirements and map controls to frameworks like the EU AI Act/NIST AI RMF via automated compliance mapping and continuous evaluator scoring [sweet.security](https://www.sweet.security/agent-security/ai-agent-security-best-practices).
- After any detected hijack or anomaly, verify rollback to baseline behavior on the next turn [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-agent-goal-hijack-in-ai-agents-4eia).

## 5. Human-in-the-Loop / Human-on-the-Loop Controls

Distinguish **human-in-the-loop** (explicit pre-approval for high-impact/irreversible actions) from **human-on-the-loop** (passive monitoring with intervention only on exceptions), and match the control model to the action's risk level [strata.io](https://www.strata.io/blog/agentic-identity/practicing-the-human-in-the-loop) [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-agent-goal-hijack-in-ai-agents-4eia). An identity-aware orchestration layer should be able to pause execution, route approvals to authorized humans, enforce time-boxed decision windows, and log every intervention [strata.io](https://www.strata.io/blog/agentic-identity/practicing-the-human-in-the-loop). Combine execution caps, scoped permissions, and policy-as-code with automated blocking/escalation when thresholds are breached [sweet.security](https://www.sweet.security/agent-security/ai-agent-security-best-practices).

---

**Bottom line**: No single control is sufficient. Effective agent security requires defense-in-depth — treating every tool call like an external API request that must be authenticated with scoped/ephemeral credentials, validated against untrusted-content assumptions, executed in strong isolation, logged immutably, and gated by human approval for high-risk actions — mapped against emerging frameworks like OWASP's Agentic Top 10, OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, and the EU AI Act.

## Key Risks and Attack Vectors for Tool-Enabled AI Agents

**1. Indirect Prompt Injection via Tool Outputs/Retrieved Content**
The core vulnerability is that LLMs cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data—both arrive as natural-language text [2]. When an agent calls a tool (web search, API, document reader), hostile instructions embedded in the returned content (web pages, emails, tickets, code repos, knowledge bases) can override the agent's original instructions [1][3][4]. This is especially dangerous in RAG, plugin, and agentic architectures where the LLM processes untrusted external content as part of its reasoning loop [3][4].

**2. Trust Boundary Collapse**
Unlike traditional software where server-side code is trusted and user input is sanitized, LLMs process both trusted system instructions and untrusted external input through the same natural-language mechanism, making it structurally hard to maintain security boundaries [5].

**3. Abuse of Tool/Function-Calling Privileges ("Toxic Agent Flows")**
Tool-augmented agents operate in cycles: detect need for external info → generate function calls → execute → incorporate results. Each tool call is a potential security boundary; if attackers manipulate tool selection or parameters via injected instructions, they can abuse the agent's privileged access [5]. A real-world example: a prompt injection flaw in GitHub's official MCP server let AI coding assistants read/write repositories without authorization, because the agent had broad permissions while processing untrusted content [5].

**4. Data Exfiltration**
A successful injection can cause the agent to leak confidential data—e.g., by crafting a tool call (such as sending an email or making an API request) that smuggles sensitive information out to an attacker-controlled destination [1][3][4].

**5. Unauthorized/Unsafe Actions via Connected Systems**
Because agentic systems can send emails, access databases, modify files, create tickets, call APIs, or trigger business workflows, a compromised instruction can cause real-world consequences far beyond simple text misbehavior—ranging from unauthorized outputs to bypassing safety policies and misusing connected tools [3][4].

**6. Log/Audit Trail Corruption**
If an attacker can silently rewrite the agent's task or constraints mid-run via injected content, downstream logs become untrustworthy, undermining the ability to reconstruct authority, intent, and alignment after the fact [2].

**7. Broader Trust/Reputational and Compliance Impact**
Beyond technical compromise, successful attacks can erode user trust, and for businesses can lead to data breaches, regulatory exposure, reputational damage, financial loss, and operational disruption [3][4].

## Recognized Mitigations/Frameworks
- Treat all user input and retrieved/tool content as untrusted; test with adversarial prompts [3][4].
- Enforce allow-lists and require human approval for privileged/high-risk tool calls [1].
- Use locked-down network access, strict access controls, and encryption to reduce the "blast radius" of injection [1].
- Cryptographically bind/sign the agent's task and constraints before untrusted content enters context, to preserve auditability [2].
- Industry frameworks formalize this risk: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications ranks prompt injection as the #1 LLM risk, and MITRE ATLAS assigns it a technique ID (AML.T0051) for threat modeling [2].

# Authentication, Authorization, and Permission-Scoping Best Practices for AI Agent Tools

## Authentication

**Use standard enterprise identity mechanisms rather than privileged agent credentials.** For actions performed on behalf of a signed-in user, employ OAuth 2.0 delegated access and flows like Microsoft Entra's On-Behalf-Of flow to preserve user identity as requests move between services. For autonomous background agents without an interactive user, use managed identities or appropriately scoped service principals [1].

**Issue ephemeral, per-task credentials.** Short-lived tokens with tool-level scopes should be used rather than long-lived static credentials, with progressive scoping built into the authorization flow [2].

**Isolate downstream credentials from the agent itself.** A connections/credential-management layer should store, refresh, rotate, and revoke OAuth tokens and API keys server-side; the agent should never directly handle raw downstream credentials [2][4]. Avoid giving the agent direct access to credentials in its execution context — the tool layer should hold credentials instead [4].

**Assign distinct credentials per agent**, not shared organizational tokens, so that permissions can be scoped per-agent and revoking one agent's access doesn't affect others [5].

**Choose the right identity model** for how the agent acts: as itself (bot/service identity, best for automation clearly attributed to a bot), as a specific user (best for acting on behalf of a user with external APIs), or under a shared org identity (fast setup, but requires additional permission layers to restrict agent access) [4].

## Authorization

**Treat the API/backend as the final authority, not the agent.** Enterprise APIs should perform their own authorization and never trust the agent's self-reported permissions; tool calls should be validated by a gateway or API layer against defined schemas, data types, and business rules before execution [1].

**Use OAuth as the authorization foundation**, combining scopes for coarse-grained limits with claims for fine-grained, context-aware authorization [3]. Restrict access tokens by audience and avoid reusing tokens across components [3].

**Use least-privilege, request-specific tokens.** Techniques like token exchange or transaction tokens should ensure APIs are called with tokens tailored to the specific request — especially important in agent-to-agent scenarios so one agent doesn't pass excessive privilege to another [3].

**Require explicit human approval for high-risk actions.** Because agent actions can diverge from user intent, high-privilege actions should trigger explicit user approval before execution [3].

**Prefer external API enforcement of permissions** by passing user-scoped tokens so the destination service (e.g., Salesforce, Google, Slack) enforces access directly — described as the strongest model, though it requires per-user OAuth connections [4].

## Permission Scoping

**Apply least privilege at the operation level.** Scope permissions by specific operation, resource, identity, and environment — e.g., read access doesn't imply write access, and create doesn't imply delete [1].

**Expose only a limited, well-defined set of tools/APIs** to the agent, ideally described with explicit schemas (e.g., OpenAPI), so the universe of possible actions is constrained upfront [1].

**Scope OAuth grants to the narrowest available permission.** Use specific scopes (e.g., `gmail.readonly` instead of `mail.google.com`) rather than broad, coarse-grained service scopes [5].

**Add a tool-level permission layer above OAuth**, since native OAuth scopes are often too coarse to express sub-service access control (e.g., Google Drive's "drive" scope grants access to all files including others' shared drives). This layer should define per-agent, per-tool policies as a hard boundary enforced at the service level — not merely a soft boundary within the agent framework, since MCP servers and agent frameworks otherwise expose all tools to every connected agent without per-caller authorization [5].

# Input Validation, Output Sanitization, and Sandboxing for Tool Calls

## Input Validation
- Treat LLM outputs/tool parameters as **untrusted at the tool level**: validate data formats (e.g., type/format parsing), enforce range limits, and cap sizes (e.g., pagination limits) before any execution occurs ([dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl)).
- In production pipelines, **input screening** (for injection attempts, PII, toxicity) should run early in the pipeline, typically within ~30ms, before the request reaches dialog/tool-access control ([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail)).
- Input validation and sanitization should **strip or flag suspicious content** before it reaches the model, as one layer in a broader defense-in-depth stack ([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail)).
- Layered controls recommended: read-only tools where possible → input validation → egress constraints → caching → circuit breakers → per-request auth → logging, so that failure in one layer is contained by others ([dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl)).
- If adopting plugin/protocol systems (e.g., MCP), add **version pinning and signature verification** ([dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl)).

## Output Sanitization / Validation
- **Output filtering** catches harmful or policy-violating content that slips past input controls, acting as a second line of defense ([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail)).
- Output validation should enforce **schema compliance**, typically within ~50ms in a production pipeline ([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail)).
- Post-validation business rules (rate limiting, audit logging) should run after output validation, typically within ~10ms ([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail)).
- Agent-generated code or shell commands should be treated as **untrusted until proven otherwise**, and routed through controlled execution rather than run directly ([YouTube - Module 2.4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WruAgVKW0tU)).

## Sandboxing Techniques
- **Isolation approaches** (in increasing strength): hardened containers (suitable only for trusted code, since they share host kernel), gVisor (user-space kernel providing syscall interception without full VM overhead), and microVMs like Firecracker/Kata Containers (strongest isolation, dedicated kernel per workload) ([northflank.com](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents)).
- Standard containers are **not sufficient** for AI-generated code execution due to shared kernel risk ([northflank.com](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents)).
- Effective sandboxing must address multiple threat vectors simultaneously: code execution exploits, filesystem access, network communication, resource consumption, and privilege escalation ([northflank.com](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents)).
- Production sandboxing requires defense-in-depth: isolation boundaries, resource limits, network controls, permission scoping, and monitoring ([northflank.com](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents)).
- Specific controls: **compute limits** to stop runaway/looping code, **file system rules** to contain probing behavior, **network controls** to restrict and log outbound calls, and **scoped, short-lived credentials/identity** to minimize blast radius if credentials leak ([YouTube - Module 2.4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WruAgVKW0tU)).
- **Privilege separation** ensures a compromised prompt/tool call cannot escalate beyond the permissions needed for its specific context ([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail)).
- Caution: sandboxes are not infallible — modern zero-day exploits increasingly target the **sandbox infrastructure itself** (hypervisor, host OS, hardware components), turning isolation into an attack vector; a layered approach beyond sandboxing alone is recommended ([menlosecurity.com](https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/what-cisos-need-to-know-about-modern-sandboxing-limitations)).

## Complementary Defense-in-Depth Layers
Beyond validation/sanitization/sandboxing, sources recommend a broader **10-layer defense-in-depth model**, including:
- Rate limiting to constrain damage from any single session
- Anomaly detection to flag deviations from normal agent behavior
- Human-in-the-loop approval for high-consequence actions
- Immutable logging/monitoring of all tool invocations and parameter changes, with attention to anomalous execution rates and unusual tool-chaining patterns (e.g., DB read followed by external transfer)
([akto.io](https://www.akto.io/blog/ai-agent-input-validation-output-guardrail); [dev.to](https://dev.to/willvelida/preventing-tool-misuse-in-ai-agents-4pcl))

research_results.findings:
Based on the provided sources, the recommended safeguards span four interconnected areas:

**1. Logging**
- Maintain **immutable logs** of all tool invocations and parameter changes, creating an audit trail for every tool call [1][4].
- Log every intervention and approval decision for auditability [2].
- Implement middleware-layer logging that captures every tool call made by the agent [3].
- Audit trails should preserve the **full delegation chain** per action — agent identity, human principal, and authorizing policy — along with the reasoning steps and tool invocations leading to each decision [4].

**2. Monitoring**
- Continuously monitor for **anomalous execution rates**, unusual tool-chaining patterns (e.g., a database read followed by an external transfer), and policy violations [1].
- Establish **behavioral baselines** for expected tool-use patterns, response lengths, and topic adherence to help detect anomalies such as goal hijacking [3].
- Monitor for tool abuse signals like unusual parameter combinations or high-frequency calls, verifying that rate limits and validation hold [3].
- Supervisors should watch for anomalies such as unusually high costs or patterns suggesting an agent chose more expensive/incorrect alternatives ("human-on-the-loop" monitoring) [2].
- Track tail latencies and cost attribution as part of production monitoring [4].
- Treat monitoring, guardrail enforcement, audit, and quantification as a **single connected program** with shared ownership rather than siloed tools [4].

**3. Auditing**
- Use **immutable log storage** retained for the period required by applicable regulatory frameworks [4].
- Apply **automated compliance mapping** to frameworks like the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF, combined with continuous evaluator scoring against sampled production traces [4].
- Include defensible rationale for human decisions as part of governance records [2].
- Conduct rollback verification after a detected hijack attempt, confirming the agent returns to baseline behavior on the next turn [3].

**4. Human-in-the-loop / Human-on-the-loop safeguards**
- Distinguish between **human-in-the-loop** (a person approves high-impact or irreversible actions before execution) and **human-on-the-loop** (a person monitors autonomous action and intervenes only on exception), matching the control model to the action's impact/risk level [5][2].
- Build an **identity-aware orchestration layer** that can pause agent execution, route approval requests to authorized humans, enforce time-boxed decision windows, and log every intervention [2].
- Route problematic traces identified through human-in-the-loop feedback into curation datasets for continuous improvement [4].
- Apply execution caps, scoped permissions, policy-as-code, and human approval thresholds, with automated blocking or escalation when thresholds are breached [5].

**Layered defense principle**
Controls should be layered (e.g., read-only tools → input validation → egress constraints → caching → circuit breakers → per-request auth → logging) so that if one layer fails, others limit the damage — treating tool calls like external API requests that must be authenticated, validated, constrained, and logged [1]. Output validation is described as the "last line of defence," scanning agent responses before they reach the user, with comprehensive logging providing the investigative trail for detected issues [3].

research_results.findings:
Based on the provided sources, the following established frameworks and standards specifically address agentic AI systems with tool/function-calling capabilities:

**OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)** – This appears to be the most directly relevant framework. It treats "instruction abuse, tool misuse, and trust boundary failures as application risks rather than abstract AI concerns" [1]. It explicitly addresses how agentic systems can have their planning hijacked, leading to execution of "privileged tool calls," persistence of malicious instructions in memory, and propagation of attacks across connected systems [3].

**OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications** – A related but distinct framework that ranks prompt injection as the top LLM risk [4] and is used to map risks such as prompt injection, sensitive data leakage, supply chain compromise, output misuse, and "excessive agency" [2].

**NIST AI Risk Management Framework** – Described as providing "a governance lens for mapping these controls to risk management" for agentic workflows, though it is noted that practical security reviews should focus on implementation details rather than staying only at this governance level [1][2].

**MITRE ATLAS** – Assigns specific technique IDs (e.g., AML.T0051 for prompt injection) that integrate into existing threat modeling practices, though the sources do not detail agent/tool-calling-specific technique coverage beyond this [4].

**EU AI Act** – Mentioned as one of the regulatory/governance frameworks that risks like excessive agency and tool/agent abuse are mapped against, alongside OWASP and NIST [2].

**Gaps in the sources:** The provided sources do not offer detailed content on NIST-specific guidance for tool/function calling, nor do they describe other frameworks (e.g., ISO/IEC standards, cloud-provider specific guidance) for agentic AI. The sources focus heavily on prompt injection as the primary lens for agentic security risk, so coverage of other tool-calling-specific risks (e.g., authentication of tool calls, sandboxing, permission scoping) is limited to general mentions of "tool misuse" and "excessive agency" [1][2][3] without granular detail.

Title: How should security teams review LLM and agent code for prompt injection risks in production workflows?
Home› FAQ› AI Security› How should security teams review LLM and agent…. # How should security teams review LLM and agent code for prompt injection risks in production workflows? Security teams should treat prompt injection as a boundary failure, not just a content issue. Review where untrusted input reaches prompts, tool calls, or agent instructions, then add sanitisation, approval gates, and strict separation between user data and system guidance. The goal is to limit what the model can see and do when instructions come from outside the trust boundary. ## Prompt Injection Becomes a Review Problem When Code Can Cross Trust Boundaries. Prompt injection is not just a model-quality issue. It becomes a production security problem when application code lets untrusted text influence system instructions, tool selection, retrieval context, or agent actions. That means reviewers need to trace data flow from user input through prompts and orchestration logic, then ask where the model could be tricked into treating attacker-controlled content as trusted guidance. For teams reviewing agentic workflows, the right reference point is how the system handles untrusted input, instruction hierarchy, and tool authority. OWASP’s OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 is useful here because it treats instruction abuse, tool misuse, and trust boundary failures as application risks rather than abstract AI concerns. ## How Security Reviews Should Trace Prompt Injection Exposure in Production. NIST’s NIST AI Risk Management Framework is relevant when teams need a governance lens for mapping these controls to risk management, but the review itself should stay close to implementation reality. The guidance breaks down when teams treat the prompt as the only security boundary and ignore the code paths that assemble, route, and execute model outputs. A model may never receive a direct malicious user prompt, but it can still ingest hostile instructions embedded in a page, ticket, or document that the application later treats as context. The exposure is highest in agentic workflows because the model is not only generating text, it is also participating in decisions that can reach external systems, data stores, or business processes. * How should security teams prevent prompt injection in AI agent workflows?

Title: How should security teams review LLM and agent code for prompt injection risks in production workflows?
Home› FAQ› AI Security› How should security teams review LLM and agent…. # How should security teams review LLM and agent code for prompt injection risks in production workflows? Security teams should treat prompt injection as a boundary failure, not just a content issue. Review where untrusted input reaches prompts, tool calls, or agent instructions, then add sanitisation, approval gates, and strict separation between user data and system guidance. The goal is to limit what the model can see and do when instructions come from outside the trust boundary. ## Prompt Injection Becomes a Review Problem When Code Can Cross Trust Boundaries. Prompt injection is not just a model-quality issue. It becomes a production security problem when application code lets untrusted text influence system instructions, tool selection, retrieval context, or agent actions. That means reviewers need to trace data flow from user input through prompts and orchestration logic, then ask where the model could be tricked into treating attacker-controlled content as trusted guidance. For teams reviewing agentic workflows, the right reference point is how the system handles untrusted input, instruction hierarchy, and tool authority. OWASP’s OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 is useful here because it treats instruction abuse, tool misuse, and trust boundary failures as application risks rather than abstract AI concerns. ## How Security Reviews Should Trace Prompt Injection Exposure in Production. NIST’s NIST AI Risk Management Framework is relevant when teams need a governance lens for mapping these controls to risk management, but the review itself should stay close to implementation reality. The guidance breaks down when teams treat the prompt as the only security boundary and ignore the code paths that assemble, route, and execute model outputs. A model may never receive a direct malicious user prompt, but it can still ingest hostile instructions embedded in a page, ticket, or document that the application later treats as context. The exposure is highest in agentic workflows because the model is not only generating text, it is also participating in decisions that can reach external systems, data stores, or business processes. * How should security teams prevent prompt injection in AI agent workflows?

# The Transformer Architecture: Evolution Since 2017

## The Original Design (2017 Baseline)

The "Attention Is All You Need" Transformer was an **encoder-decoder** architecture built entirely on attention, with design choices that later changed: **post-norm** (LayerNorm applied *after* the residual addition), **absolute sinusoidal positional encodings**, **full multi-head scaled dot-product attention** (self-attention in the encoder, masked self-attention plus cross-attention in the decoder), and a **plain feedforward layer** (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SnbFev7N4yM, https://theorempath.com/compare/pre-norm-vs-post-norm, https://medium.com/@lmpo/transformers-explained-why-attention-is-truly-all-you-need-2e3669242965, https://haroldbenoit.com/notes/ml/llms/architecture/encoder-decoder-models).

## The Biggest Structural Change: Encoder-Decoder → Decoder-Only (and Encoder-Only)

Beyond swapping components inside each block, the field also abandoned the original **encoder-decoder** skeleton itself for most applications. BERT stripped out the decoder to build an encoder-only, bidirectional model for representation learning, while GPT and essentially all subsequent large generative models (LLaMA, Mistral, etc.) stripped out the encoder to build decoder-only, causally-masked autoregressive models. One source describes the resulting convergence explicitly: "many Transformer architectures have converged toward a LLaMA-like design — a stack of attention and feed-forward layers connected by residuals," with decoder-only stacks becoming the de facto template and remaining variation confined to normalization type and layer layout (https://medium.com/@ashutoshs81127/why-pre-norm-became-the-default-in-transformers-4229047e2620). This decoder-only pattern is now ubiquitous across the model families discussed throughout the research — GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, OLMo, Falcon, and the MoE-based GPT-OSS and Llama 4 (https://sebastianraschka.com/faq/docs/swiglu-modern-llms.html, https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/feature/12-of-the-best-large-language-models).

This matters for how we should read the "stable skeleton" framing used elsewhere: it's accurate *within* a given architecture family (decoder-only models haven't changed their residual block silhouette much since GPT/LLaMA), but it glosses over the fact that the field first discarded half of the original 2017 skeleton (the encoder-decoder split itself) before that narrower decoder-only skeleton stabilized. Several researchers treat this encoder-decoder-to-decoder-only shift as one of the most consequential post-2017 changes precisely because it became the near-universal template that enabled the scaling-era LLM boom.

**Important caveat:** the available research could not establish, from citable sources, the specific mechanics of *why* decoder-only won out over encoder-only or encoder-decoder for generative modeling (e.g., training/inference simplicity, better scaling behavior for next-token prediction) — this rationale is widely discussed in the field but is not substantiated in the sources gathered here, so it is flagged as a gap rather than asserted. Likewise, no source in this research explicitly details BERT's bidirectional masked-attention mechanics versus GPT's causal masking as a point-by-point comparison; only the end-state convergence toward decoder-only designs is directly supported (https://medium.com/@ashutoshs81127/why-pre-norm-became-the-default-in-transformers-4229047e2620). Other architectural variants explored along the way — Evolved Transformers (convolutional sublayers) and Universal Transformers (recurrent parameter sharing) — are mentioned as having existed but did not become dominant (https://haroldbenoit.com/notes/ml/llms/architecture/encoder-decoder-models).

## Component-Level Changes Within the (Now Decoder-Only) Block

**Normalization:** Post-norm gave way to **pre-norm** (normalization before the sublayer, inside the residual branch), providing cleaner gradient flow and more stable training in deep networks — now the default (https://medium.com/@ashutoshs81127/why-pre-norm-became-the-default-in-transformers-4229047e2620, https://mbrenndoerfer.com/writing/pre-norm-vs-post-norm). LayerNorm was often replaced by the simpler, faster **RMSNorm**, popularized by LLaMA as part of the "Pre-LN + RMSNorm + SwiGLU + RoPE" combination later adopted by Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and OLMo — though Falcon notably stuck with full LayerNorm after its own ablations, showing RMSNorm isn't universally superior (https://sebastianraschka.com/faq/docs/swiglu-modern-llms.html). A newer "Double Norm" pattern (Pre-Norm plus an extra post-block LayerNorm) appears in Grok and Gemma 2, and QK-Norm and logit soft-capping were added as extra stability guardrails (https://medium.com/@wasowski.jarek/s01e10-a-decade-of-misplaced-sacred-cows-in-neural-networks-residuals-norms-1a4f85749a0d).

**Positional encoding:** Absolute sinusoidal encodings gave way to relative schemes — T5's learned relative position bias, then **Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)**, now the dominant approach for modern decoder-only and encoder-decoder models, alongside alternatives like ALiBi and refinements like StableMask (https://haroldbenoit.com/notes/ml/llms/architecture/encoder-decoder-models, https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/decoder-only-transformer-architecture). RoPE-scaling techniques (Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) were later developed to extend context length (https://hassannazir.dev/blogs/deep-learning-transformers-attention-mechanisms-2025).

**Feedforward network:** The plain FFN evolved into gated variants — **SwiGLU** (and GeGLU) — which improved language-modeling performance over ReLU/GELU FFNs and became standard in LLaMA-style architectures (https://dev.to/mshojaei77/swiglu-the-ffn-upgrade-i-use-to-get-free-performance-33jc, https://sebastianraschka.com/faq/docs/swiglu-modern-llms.html). Under scaling pressure, dense FFNs were in some models replaced by **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** layers — routing tokens to expert sub-networks — adopted in Switch Transformer, Llama 4, and GPT-OSS (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SnbFev7N4yM, https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/feature/12-of-the-best-large-language-models).

**Attention mechanism:** A long efficiency-focused progression emerged to cut KV-cache size and compute cost: **Multi-Query Attention (MQA)** → **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)**, now standard in Falcon, Llama 2, Mistral, Mixtral → **Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)** for further KV-cache compression (https://tinkerd.net/blog/machine-learning/multi-query-attention, https://haroldbenoit.com/notes/ml/llms/architecture/encoder-decoder-models). Alongside these, **sliding-window/sparse/local attention** limits cost at long context, and **linear attention** and **state-space models** (Mamba) offer linear-time alternatives, with hybrids like Jamba and Qwen3-Next interleaving full attention with linear-time layers (https://hassannazir.dev/blogs/deep-learning-transformers-attention-mechanisms-2025). Separately, **FlashAttention** is a pure I/O/engineering optimization — same math, far less memory traffic — now widely deployed in production (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.07247v1).

## Which Changes Mattered Most

Four changes stand out as the strongest candidates for "most impactful," spanning both the architectural-skeleton level and the intra-block level:

1. **The encoder-decoder → decoder-only (and encoder-only/BERT) split.** This is arguably the most consequential change of all, since it redefined the overall model skeleton that later component swaps operated within, and became the near-universal template for scaling generative LLMs (https://medium.com/@ashutoshs81127/why-pre-norm-became-the-default-in-transformers-4229047e2620). It is flagged with the caveat above that the detailed rationale for its dominance was not directly substantiated in this research.
2. **Efficient attention variants (GQA, MLA, sliding-window attention, FlashAttention)** — these address the Transformer's core bottleneck, quadratic attention cost, and are central enough to warrant dedicated benchmarking studies; FlashAttention is hardware-optimized and ubiquitous in production (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.07247v1).
3. **SwiGLU** — a low-risk, low-effort swap that became "the GLU variant that won out," now near-universal in SOTA FFN design (https://dev.to/mshojaei77/swiglu-the-ffn-upgrade-i-use-to-get-free-performance-33jc).
4. **RoPE** — now the default positional scheme for long-context, decoder-only models, enabling extrapolation that absolute encodings could not achieve (https://haroldbenoit.com/notes/ml/llms/architecture/encoder-decoder-models).

A fifth, emerging development worth flagging is **hybrid state-space/attention architectures** (Mamba-style selective SSMs combined with attention), which have moved from research into production — e.g., AI21's Jamba 1.5 achieving a 10x KV-cache memory reduction at 256K context, and NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 committing to hybrid Mamba-transformer designs — suggesting this could be the next major structural shift (https://medium.com/@marc.bara.iniesta/the-post-transformer-breakthrough-will-arrive-by-early-2027-ccfe791be5b5).

One synthesis frames the intra-block changes (pre-norm/RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA/MLA, SwiGLU/MoE) as responses to four pressures — stability, context length, inference cost, and scaling — while treating the residual-block structure as a fixed "skyscraper" silhouette (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SnbFev7N4yM). That framing holds within the decoder-only family that now dominates the field, but it understates the earlier, more fundamental break: before that skeleton stabilized, the field discarded the original encoder-decoder split altogether in favor of encoder-only (BERT) and, overwhelmingly, decoder-only (GPT/LLaMA-style) designs.

---

This leaves the subtask's core question largely unanswered despite it being well within the scope of commonly available literature. - The write-up states as established fact that 'BERT stripped out the decoder to build an encoder-only, bidirectional model' and that 'GPT and essentially all subsequent large generative models... stripped out the encoder to build decoder-only, causally-masked autoregressive models,' citing only a source about convergence toward LLaMA-like designs. However, subtask s3's findings explicitly flag this exact claim (BERT's encoder-only bidirectional design vs. GPT's decoder-only causal design, and the general encoder-decoder-to-decoder-only split) as NOT supported by any retrieved source — it was marked as a gap. records.query: How has the transformer architecture changed since 2017, and which changes mattered most?

research_results.findings:
Based on the provided sources, the original 2017 Transformer architecture from "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al.) had the following key design choices:

**Overall structure**: An encoder-decoder architecture built entirely on attention mechanisms, replacing recurrence and convolutions with self-attention, enabling parallelization that RNNs/LSTMs could not achieve [4].

**Input representation**: Token embeddings via a learned embedding matrix, combined with **absolute positional encodings** using fixed **sinusoidal functions** (since the architecture lacks recurrence and needs some way to inject sequence order information) [2][4].

**Attention mechanism**: **Multi-head scaled dot-product self-attention**. In the encoder, Q, K, V are all derived from the same input sequence (self-attention); the decoder also uses masked self-attention and cross-attention [2][4]. The course materials describe this as the core innovation that "weights different positions of an input sequence to compute an output sequence" [3].

**Normalization placement**: The original architecture used **post-norm**, meaning normalization was applied *after* the residual addition: 
xₗ₊₁ = LayerNorm(xₗ + Sublayer(xₗ))
This is explicitly contrasted with later "pre-norm" designs (used in GPT-2, LLaMA, PaLM) where normalization is applied before the sublayer [5].

**Feedforward structure**: A "plain" feedforward layer — later described as the baseline that was eventually superseded by gated variants like SwiGLU in subsequent architectures [1].

**Legacy/retrofitting context**: One source frames the original 2017 design as a stable "backbone" that has persisted structurally (residual connections, overall block silhouette) even as individual components were later modified — e.g., post-norm → pre-norm/RMSNorm, sinusoidal positional encoding → RoPE, full multi-head attention → grouped query attention/multi-latent attention, and plain feedforward → SwiGLU/Mixture-of-Experts — all while the residual "highway" and block structure remained unchanged [1].

The sources do not provide additional specifics from the original paper itself (e.g., exact number of layers, d_model size, number of heads), beyond these architectural design choices.

The Transformer architecture revolutionized artificial intelligence by rendering previous recurrent models obsolete. By replacing recurrence with pure attention, it eliminated sequential bottlenecks, solved vanishing gradients, and enabled unprecedented parallelization. research_results.findings:
Based on the provided sources, since the original 2017 Transformer, significant architectural innovations have emerged in two main areas: positional encoding and attention mechanism efficiency.

## Positional Encoding Changes

The original Transformer used fixed or learned **absolute positional embeddings**, but these have largely been superseded due to limitations in generalizing to longer sequences [1][2]:

- **Relative position encodings**: T5 introduced a relative position bias scheme using learned bias buckets, moving away from absolute embeddings for greater flexibility [1].
- **Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)**: Introduced by Su et al. (2024), RoPE provides continuous relative positioning and has become a recommended approach for modern encoder-decoder and decoder-only models [1][2].
- **ALiBi**: Used as an alternative relative position encoding scheme in decoder-only architectures [2].
- **StableMask**: A masking refinement (Yin et al., 2024) that addresses a known limitation of relative position schemes—their inability to encode absolute position for universal approximation—making decoder-only architectures more suitable for position-sensitive domains like code and mathematics [2].
- **RoPE scaling techniques**: Methods like Position Interpolation (PI), NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN have been developed specifically to extend RoPE-based models to longer context lengths [5].
- **Disjoint positional encodings**: Used in streaming/simultaneous translation decoder-only models to enable prefix-to-prefix translation policies [2].

General trend: relative/rotary schemes improve generalization to longer sequences and training stability compared to absolute embeddings, which limit extrapolation beyond trained sequence lengths [1].

## Attention Mechanism Changes

A progression of efficiency-focused attention variants has emerged, primarily to reduce KV-cache size and computational cost [3][4][5]:

- **Multi-Query Attention (MQA)**: Introduced (Shazeer, 2019) to reduce KV cache size by sharing key/value projections across all query heads [3][5].
- **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)**: A generalization of MQA (introduced October 2023) that groups query heads to share KV projections, balancing efficiency and performance; adopted in Falcon, Llama 2, Mistral, and Mixtral models [3][4].
- **Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA)**: A further evolution for KV cache compression [3][5].
- **Local/sliding-window attention, sink, and sparse attention**: Approaches that cut computational costs for long contexts by limiting the attention scope [3][5].
- **Linear attention**: Replaces the quadratic attention score matrix with more efficient formulations [3][5].
- **State-space and linear-attention models**: Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) introduced selective state-space layers enabling linear-time sequence processing; hybrid architectures like Jamba (Mamba + attention) and Qwen3-Next (2025, mixing Gated DeltaNet with gated attention) interleave full-attention layers with linear-time layers to handle very long contexts while retaining precise recall [5].
- **FlashAttention**: An engineering-level optimization that reduces memory traffic/IO cost without changing the mathematical output of attention, making it faster to compute at scale [5].

## Overall Trend

Sources indicate that most architectural progress between 2023–2026 has not replaced the core attention operation itself, but rather focused on making it "cheaper to store, faster to compute, and able to see further" [5]. The combination of GQA/MLA (shrinking KV cache) + FlashAttention (reducing memory traffic) + RoPE scaling (enabling longer context) + sparse/sliding-window/sink attention (reducing cost of long context) represents the current state of practical attention engineering [5].

research_results.findings:
Based on the provided sources, here is a summary of the key architectural changes in transformers since 2017:

**Normalization placement: Post-LN → Pre-LN (and beyond)**
The original 2017 Transformer used Post-Norm (LayerNorm applied after the residual addition). Over time, most models moved to Pre-Norm (normalization before attention/FFN sublayers, inside the residual branch), which produces cleaner gradient flow and more stable training, especially for deep networks [1][3]. This shift from post-norm to pre-norm is described as one of the major retrofits to the architecture [3]. One source recommends "Pre-LN (or Peri-LN for deep models)" as the 2026 standard, noting it "preserves the clean gradient highway" [2].

A more recent trend, "Double Norm," adds LayerNorm both before *and* after each block (Pre-Norm + an extra post-block LayerNorm). Grok and Gemma 2 are cited as adopters of this pattern [1].

**Normalization type: LayerNorm → RMSNorm**
RMSNorm (a simplified normalization that drops the mean-centering step) has become the de facto standard, "faster, equally effective," since its adoption by LLaMA [2]. LLaMA 1 (Feb 2023) is credited as the breakthrough that established the combination "Pre-LN + RMSNorm + SwiGLU + RoPE," subsequently adopted by Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and OLMo [2]. Falcon (TII) is noted as an exception, choosing full LayerNorm after ablations, showing the RMSNorm choice isn't universally superior [2].

Additional normalization innovations mentioned include QK-Norm (normalizing query/key projections, described as cheap insurance against training instability) and logit soft-capping [2][3]. A newer alternative, DyT (Dynamic Tanh), and its December 2025 successor "Derf" (using erf(αx + s)) are mentioned as experimental but not yet used in any production LLM [2].

**Activation functions / feedforward structure: plain FFN → gated GLU variants**
The plain feedforward layer (originally ReLU-based, later GELU in models like BERT) has evolved into gated linear unit (GLU) variants such as GeGLU and SwiGLU [3][4][5]. SwiGLU computes two projections of the input, applies SiLU (Swish) activation to one, multiplies them elementwise, then projects back down — this gating mechanism improved language-modeling results over plain ReLU/GELU FFNs in matched training setups, per the "GLU Variants Improve Transformer" research, and was adopted into Llama-style architectures as part of a broader set of changes [5][3][4]. This is described as the feedforward layer "gaining a gate" and becoming SwiGLU "under scaling" pressure [3].

**Feedforward/block structure: dense FFN → Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)**
Under scaling pressure, the dense feedforward layer in some architectures has been replaced or supplemented by Mixture-of-Experts layers, where the FFN slot is "federated into experts" — multiple expert sub-networks with routing, rather than a single dense FFN per block [3].

**Broader framing**
One source frames all these changes (norm placement, gating in FFN, RoPE for positions, GQA/MLA for attention efficiency, MoE for scaling) as responses to four pressures: stability, context, inference cost, and scaling — while the overall residual "skyscraper" backbone and block silhouette of the original Transformer have remained unchanged; only what happens inside each slot has changed [3][2].

What is SwiGLU, and why is it common in modern LLM feed-forward layers?
SwiGLU is a gated feed-forward layer. It computes two projections of the same token representation, applies the SiLU activation to one projection, multiplies the two paths element by element, and projects the result back to the model width.
This differs from using SiLU by itself. SiLU, also called Swish, is the activation function
\[\operatorname{SiLU}(z)=z\,\sigma(z).\] [...] For the broader block-level transition, see What architectural changes turned GPT-style models into Llama-style models?. The related mixture-of-experts FAQ explains the separate expert-routing mechanism.

Based on the provided sources, here is what can be established — with explicit notes on gaps.

## BERT vs. GPT vs. original Transformer — structural differences

The sources confirm the general schema but contain **limited direct detail** on BERT's or GPT's specific structural divergence from the original encoder-decoder Transformer.

- The original Transformer (2017) was an **encoder-decoder** architecture. Encoder-decoder models use an encoder stack and decoder stack, with positional encoding, attention, and normalization choices varying across variants [2].
- On architectural variants broadly, source [2] notes that beyond the standard Transformer, researchers explored efficiency variants: **Evolved Transformers** (convolutional sublayers), **Universal Transformers** (parameter sharing across time steps/recurrent updates), and **Mixture-of-Experts** (conditional routing to feed-forward experts) [2]. This source does not specifically break down BERT's bidirectional masked-LM encoder-only design or GPT's causal decoder-only design in structural terms.
- Source [4] and [5] reference GPT-series and decoder-only models in the context of scaling and MoE adoption (e.g., GPT-OSS using MoE, Llama 4 moving to MoE) but do not detail the original architectural shift from encoder-decoder to decoder-only causal attention [4].
- Source [1] discusses the general "retrofitting" of the transformer block (norm placement, attention mechanisms, FFN gating, MoE) under four pressures — stability, context, inference, and scaling — but does not explicitly contrast BERT's bidirectional attention against GPT's causal attention, nor explain why decoder-only became dominant [1].

**Gap**: None of the provided sources explicitly state that BERT removed the decoder and used bidirectional/masked-token attention, or that GPT removed the encoder and used unidirectional causal attention, nor do they explain the simplification rationale for decoder-only dominance (e.g., training efficiency, scaling simplicity for autoregressive generation). This specific comparison is not covered in the given materials.

## Why decoder-only became dominant (Llama, GPT, Mistral)

The sources provide only indirect evidence:
- Source [3] notes that "many Transformer architectures have converged toward a LLaMA-like design — a stack of attention and feed-forward layers connected by residuals," suggesting decoder-only stacks became a de facto template, with remaining variation in normalization (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm) and layout (serial vs. parallel) [3].
- Source [5] frames architectural evolution in "three waves" tied to scaling challenges, implying decoder-only architectures suited scaling-driven simplification, but the excerpt is cut off before elaborating [5].

**Gap**: No source directly explains *why* decoder-only architectures became dominant over encoder-decoder for generative LLMs.

## Long-context architectures beyond RoPE/sliding-window

The provided sources do **not** mention Longformer, BigBird, or other sparse/local-attention long-context architectures by name. Source [1] only references "long-context scaling" and RoPE/sliding window attention as mechanisms for context handling, without naming Longformer- or BigBird-style sparse attention patterns [1]. Source [2] discusses positional encoding evolution (absolute → relative → RoPE) as relevant to length generalization but does not discuss Longformer/BigBird-style architectures [2].

**Gap**: The supplied sources contain no information on Longformer, BigBird, or other dedicated long-context sparse-attention architectures. This cannot be answered from the given material.

One of the most interesting design debates revolves around a seemingly small detail:
👉 Where should we place Layer Normalization in a Transformer block?
This choice — known as Pre-Norm vs Post-Normhas shaped the evolution of every major Transformer model since 2017.   
Let’s unpack what it means, why it matters, and what new innovations are emerging.
🧠 Setting the Stage: Variations in Modern Transformers [...] Over the past few years, many Transformer architectures have converged toward a LLaMA-like design — a stack of attention and feed-forward layers connected by residuals.
Still, there’s no perfect consensus on all the details.   
Different models mix things up:  
_- Some use__LayerNorm__, while others prefer__RMSNorm__(a simpler normalization variant).  
Some use__serial__versus__parallel__layer layouts.  
Some tweak activation functions or hidden sizes._ [...] 🔄 The Latest Innovation: “Double Norm”
Image 8
Even though Pre-Norm dominates today, researchers haven’t stopped experimenting.  
A recent trend introduces a twist: adding an extra LayerNorm at the end of each block.
This design — sometimes called Double Norm — looks like this:
1.   Apply LayerNorm before attention (like Pre-Norm).
2.   Apply another LayerNorm _after_ the block.
Recent models adopting this:
   Grok and Gemma 2→ LayerNorm before _and_ after each block.

research_results.findings:
Based on the provided sources, the following post-2017 transformer modifications stand out as most impactful by the three criteria (adoption in SOTA models, performance/efficiency gains, influence on subsequent research):

**1. Efficient/modified attention mechanisms (Grouped Query Attention, Sliding Window Attention, Flash Attention, Multi-head Latent Attention/MLA)**
These are explicitly grouped together as the primary line of research addressing the original Transformer's main limitation—the quadratic time/memory complexity of self-attention [1][4]. The source notes these "aim to reduce resource consumption while maintaining model performance" and are significant enough to be the subject of dedicated comparative benchmarking studies, indicating their centrality to current research and deployment [4]. Flash Attention in particular is highlighted as a hardware-optimized (NVIDIA) solution, pointing to its practical adoption in production systems [4].

**2. SwiGLU feed-forward network upgrade**
SwiGLU, a variant of Gated Linear Units (GLU) that replaces the standard ReLU/GELU activation in the FFN sublayer with a Swish-gated mechanism, is characterized as having become the dominant choice among GLU variants ("the one that won out") [2]. It is described as a "low-effort, low-risk" change that aligns new models with "proven, state-of-the-art architectures," suggesting widespread adoption in contemporary SOTA model design [2].

**3. Hybrid state-space/attention architectures (Mamba-style selective SSMs combined with sparse/local attention)**
While not a modification of the Transformer per se, hybrid architectures combining selective state space blocks with attention are described as having "moved from research to production," citing concrete adoption such as AI21's Jamba 1.5 (256K context, 10x KV-cache memory reduction) and NVIDIA's committed shift to hybrid Mamba-transformer designs for its Nemotron 3 family [3]. This represents a significant efficiency-driven evolution influencing next-generation model design, with reported results showing a 7B hybrid model outperforming reasoning models seven times its size at nearly double the throughput [3].

**Caveat:** The provided sources do not directly address other commonly discussed post-2017 modifications (e.g., RMSNorm, rotary positional embeddings/RoPE, pre-layer normalization) despite these being frequently cited elsewhere in the literature — the search results simply do not cover them, so no claim can be made about their relative impact based on this source set [1][2][3][4][5].

My Opinion
In my opinion, if you're building a new Transformer from scratch in 2024 or fine-tuning an older architecture, swapping the FFN for a properly-dimensioned SwiGLU block is one of the highest-ROI changes you can make. It's a low-effort, low-risk upgrade that aligns your model with proven, state-of-the-art architectures. [...] Gated Linear Units (arXiv:1612.08083) consist of the component-wise product of two linear projections, one of which is first passed through a sigmoid function. Variations on GLU are possible, using different nonlinear (or even linear) functions in place of sigmoid. We test these variants in the feed-forward sublayers of the Transformer (arXiv:1706.03762) sequence-to-sequence model, and find that some of them yield quality improvements over the typically-used ReLU or GELU activations. [...] This dynamic, data-dependent filtering is more powerful than a static ReLU. It allows the network to route information more intelligently. The original GLU paper spawned several variants, including ReGLU (ReLU gate) and GEGLU (GELU gate). The one that won out is SwiGLU.
2. The Math That Matters: What is SwiGLU?
SwiGLU simply replaces the sigmoid function in the GLU's gate with another activation: Swish (also known as SiLU in PyTorch).

Every large language model you use is built around one operation: attention. Most of the architectural progress in LLMs from 2023 to 2026 has not replaced it. It has made attention cheaper to store, faster to compute, and able to see further.
This guide walks through the math, then through the engineering changes that matter when you run these models in production.
1. Scaled Dot-Product Attention [...] State-space and linear-attention models replace the quadratic score matrix with a recurrent state that has constant size per layer:
 Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) introduced selective state-space layers with linear-time sequence processing.
 Hybrid architectures interleave a minority of full-attention layers with many linear-time layers. Examples include AI21's Jamba (Mamba plus attention) and Qwen3-Next (2025), which mixes Gated DeltaNet layers with gated attention. [...] GQA and MLA shrink the KV cache; FlashAttention reduces memory traffic without changing results.
 RoPE scaling (PI, NTK, YaRN) enables longer contexts; sliding-window, sink, and sparse attention cut the cost of using them.
 Hybrid linear-attention models are the main architectural bet for very long contexts, with full-attention layers kept for precise recall.
References

One of the most interesting design debates revolves around a seemingly small detail:
👉 Where should we place Layer Normalization in a Transformer block?
This choice — known as Pre-Norm vs Post-Normhas shaped the evolution of every major Transformer model since 2017.   
Let’s unpack what it means, why it matters, and what new innovations are emerging.
🧠 Setting the Stage: Variations in Modern Transformers [...] Over the past few years, many Transformer architectures have converged toward a LLaMA-like design — a stack of attention and feed-forward layers connected by residuals.
Still, there’s no perfect consensus on all the details.   
Different models mix things up:  
_- Some use__LayerNorm__, while others prefer__RMSNorm__(a simpler normalization variant).  
Some use__serial__versus__parallel__layer layouts.  
Some tweak activation functions or hidden sizes._ [...] 🔄 The Latest Innovation: “Double Norm”
Image 8
Even though Pre-Norm dominates today, researchers haven’t stopped experimenting.  
A recent trend introduces a twist: adding an extra LayerNorm at the end of each block.
This design — sometimes called Double Norm — looks like this:
1.   Apply LayerNorm before attention (like Pre-Norm).
2.   Apply another LayerNorm _after_ the block.
Recent models adopting this:
   Grok and Gemma 2→ LayerNorm before _and_ after each block.

Image 11: The complete “skyscraper recipe” — compare it against the architectural card of any LLM.
_The complete “skyscraper recipe” — compare it against the architectural card of any LLM._
The recommendation for 2026 is clear:
   Pre-LN (or Peri-LN for deep models) — preserves the clean gradient highway
   RMSNorm — faster, equally effective, the standard since LLaMA
   QK-Norm — two lines of code protecting against weeks of wasted GPU
   Gradient clipping with max_norm=1.0 — safety net [...] In December 2025, Derf appeared — a DyT successor using erf(alphax + s), claiming even better results. The field is evolving rapidly. The caveat matters: no production LLM uses DyT yet. RMSNorm + Pre-LN remains the safe choice for 2026. DyT is a warning signal — “obvious” architectural assumptions can be wrong.
> _“Theory without practice is barren, practice without theory is blind.” — Immanuel Kant, Philosopher_
The Recipe for a Skyscraper That Stands — Recommendations for 2026 [...] LLaMA 1 (February 2023) was the adoption breakthrough. Meta established the “recipe”: Pre-LN + RMSNorm + SwiGLU + RoPE. From that point, virtually every new open-source model — Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, OLMo — adopted RMSNorm. The exception is Falcon (TII), which after ablations chose full LayerNorm — proof that standard modern choices aren’t universally better.

SwiGLU belongs to the family studied in GLU Variants Improve Transformer. In those experiments, gated variants improved Transformer language-modeling results compared with plain ReLU or GELU feed-forward layers under matched training setups. What is SwiGLU, and why is it common in modern LLM feed-forward layers?
SwiGLU is a gated feed-forward layer. It computes two projections of the same token representation, applies the SiLU activation to one projection, multiplies the two paths element by element, and projects the result back to the model width.
This differs from using SiLU by itself. SiLU, also called Swish, is the activation function

sources.snippet: In June 2017, a team of researchers from Google Brain and Google Research published "Attention Is All You Need," introducing the Transformer architecture that would fundamentally reshape natural language processing and become the foundation for virtually all modern language AI systems. The paper presented a novel architecture that eliminated recurrence and convolution entirely, relying solely on attention mechanisms to process sequences. This seemingly radical simplification would prove to be [...] The Transformer architecture had several limitations that would shape subsequent research directions. Perhaps the most significant was the quadratic computational complexity of self-attention relative to sequence length. Computing attention over a sequence of length  requires computing attention scores for all  pairs of positions, which becomes computationally expensive for very long sequences. This quadratic complexity limited the practical sequence lengths that transformers could handle [...] Despite the success of LSTM-based neural machine translation systems, researchers in 2017 were confronting fundamental limitations that stemmed from the sequential processing inherent in recurrent architectures. LSTM networks process sequences one position at a time, with each step depending on the previous step's computation. This sequential dependency created several critical bottlenecks that limited both the practical scalability of these models and their theoretical capacity to capture

My Opinion
In my opinion, if you're building a new Transformer from scratch in 2024 or fine-tuning an older architecture, swapping the FFN for a properly-dimensioned SwiGLU block is one of the highest-ROI changes you can make. It's a low-effort, low-risk upgrade that aligns your model with proven, state-of-the-art architectures. [...] Gated Linear Units (arXiv:1612.08083) consist of the component-wise product of two linear projections, one of which is first passed through a sigmoid function. Variations on GLU are possible, using different nonlinear (or even linear) functions in place of sigmoid. We test these variants in the feed-forward sublayers of the Transformer (arXiv:1706.03762) sequence-to-sequence model, and find that some of them yield quality improvements over the typically-used ReLU or GELU activations. [...] This dynamic, data-dependent filtering is more powerful than a static ReLU. It allows the network to route information more intelligently. The original GLU paper spawned several variants, including ReGLU (ReLU gate) and GEGLU (GELU gate). The one that won out is SwiGLU.
2. The Math That Matters: What is SwiGLU?
SwiGLU simply replaces the sigmoid function in the GLU's gate with another activation: Swish (also known as SiLU in PyTorch).
